Exercise Deep Specification
Exercise 1 — Word Association
Day 10 · Universal · Replaces Emotional Vocabulary Wheel
Attribute
Value
Exercise ID
EX-01
Trigger
Day 10 of Cycle 1 (day-based unlock, no entry minimum)
Runs
Once per Cycle 1. Not repeated in subsequent cycles.
Completion time
5–8 minutes
Question count
12 stimulus words (9 fixed + 2–3 personalised)
Response type
Free text — one word or short phrase per stimulus

Audience for this doc
Developer (Bubble) + Designer (UI/UX) — both simultaneously
1. What It Collects

The Word Association exercise collects 12 free-text responses to stimulus words — one response per word, written before deliberation can set in. The stimulus set is partly fixed (9 core words, identical for every user) and partly personalised (2–3 words drawn from the user's own first 9 journal entries). The user never knows which words are fixed and which are personalised.

What the exercise is actually measuring: the gap between instinctive emotional associations and the language the user chooses in their journal entries. A user who responds 'always me' to WRONG but whose entries never assign self-blame — that gap is more revealing than either data point alone.
1.1 The Fixed Core Set — 9 Words
These 9 words appear for every user in every Cycle 1, in the fixed positions shown. They are sequenced deliberately — see Section 6.1 for rationale.
Word (Position)
What it probes
What a deflected or revealing response looks like
HOME (1)
Attachment, safety, belonging — baseline relational orientation

Neutral or architectural responses ('a building', 'my flat') flag emotional detachment from relational context. Warm, person-referencing responses ('mum', 'where I feel safe') signal relational baseline.
ANGER (2)
Relationship to strong negative affect — owned, projected, or suppressed
Deflection to others ('my dad', 'traffic', 'unfair') vs. ownership ('me when cornered', 'necessary') is the primary signal. Blanket negatives ('bad', 'avoid it') suggest suppression.
ENOUGH (4)
Self-sufficiency, adequacy, scarcity — core locus-of-control marker
Outward responses ('never', 'hard to find', 'not for me') map onto low agency. Inward responses ('I am', 'usually', 'most days') map onto higher agency. SA dimension feed.
SAFE (6)
Emotional safety model — what safety requires, who provides it
Abstract responses ('money', 'routine', 'locked doors') vs. relational ones ('her', 'being understood', 'honesty') flag suppression profile. Purely material safety = emotional safety model absent.
WAITING (7)
Passive orientation, anticipated future, locus of control in time
Dread responses ('dread', 'always', 'my whole life') vs. neutral patience ('okay', 'sometimes') vs. resentment ('wasted time') map onto DT and SA dimensions.
WRONG (8)
Self-blame vs. external attribution, shame surface

First-person ownership ('me', 'I was', 'I got it wrong') vs. external attribution ('them', 'the situation', 'unfair') is a direct SA dimension marker. High self-blame + low SA in entries = strong signal.
CLOSE (10)
Relational proximity — desired, feared, or ambivalent

Physical interpretation ('near', 'distance', 'shut') vs. relational ('trust', 'vulnerable', 'her') flags emotional avoidance of intimacy. Negative relational responses ('dangerous', 'too much') relevant to Branch A.
STILL (11)
Internal quietude vs. stagnation — how rest is experienced
Peaceful associations ('calm', 'finally', 'breath') vs. trapped/stuck associations ('going nowhere', 'stagnant', 'bored') distinguish emotional baseline and DT direction.
BREAK (12)
Rest vs. rupture — same word holds both; which meaning surfaces first

Rest-oriented responses ('holiday', 'sleep', 'space') vs. rupture-oriented ('snap', 'apart', 'end it') show whether relief is associated with separation or rest. Rupture responses at position 12 are notable.
1.2 The Personalised Words — 2–3 from Entries (Positions 3, 5, 9)

2–3 words are selected from the user's first 9 journal entries by Call 1 (Section 2.4). They are inserted at positions 3, 5, and 9 — splitting the fixed words so the personalised words feel continuous with the sequence, not appended.

Selection criteria: appeared in multiple entries, carried visible emotional charge in context, not already in the fixed set, not proper nouns or highly specific references, common enough to be a recognisable stimulus. If only 2 words meet all criteria, 2 are used and position 9 remains a fixed word (STILL moves to 9, BREAK to 12).
DEVELOPER NOTE

The personalised word positions (3, 5, 9) are fixed in the sequence template. Call 1 returns up to 3 words. The workflow inserts them into these positions and stores the final 12-word sequence in a draft ExerciseResult record before the exercise unlocks on Day 10. Positions 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 10, 11, 12 are always fixed words. Position 3, 5, 9 are personalised slots. If Call 1 returns only 2 words, slot 9 uses STILL (shifted from position 11) and slot 11 uses CLOSE (shifted from position 10). The full 12-word sequence becomes: 1=HOME, 2=ANGER, 3=personalised, 4=ENOUGH, 5=personalised, 6=SAFE, 7=WAITING, 8=WRONG, 9=STILL, 10=BREAK, 11=CLOSE, 12=(removed — exercise runs 11 words). CORRECTION: to always maintain exactly 12 words, add CHANGE as position 12 when only 2 personalised words are returned. Final sequence with 2 words: 1=HOME, 2=ANGER, 3=personalised, 4=ENOUGH, 5=personalised, 6=SAFE, 7=WAITING, 8=WRONG, 9=STILL, 10=CLOSE, 11=BREAK, 12=CHANGE. This preserves the closing trio structure with BREAK at position 11 and adds a neutral final word.
1.3 What Each Response Is Scored Against

Individual responses are not scored in isolation. The AI (Call 2) reads all 12 responses together and assesses two things: the consistent emotional register across the full set, and the gap between that register and the emotional language visible in the user's journal entries.
Output field
What it captures
Dominant register

The consistent emotional orientation across all 12 responses: threat/self-questioning, withdrawal/accommodation, direct expression, avoidant detachment, or ambivalent/mixed. This is the primary routing signal.
Emotional register gap

Whether the register visible in responses matches the emotional language in entries: match (consistent), partial (some divergence), or significant gap (responses reveal territory absent from entries). This feeds EI score calibration.
2–3 most revealing pairs
The specific stimulus-response pairs the AI flags as most revealing of the dominant register. Referenced directly in the Day 30 report.
Suppression flag
Set to Yes if: significant gap between response register and entry language, AND responses contain high-intensity emotional content that entries consistently avoid. Feeds Branch C routing.
2. How It Collects
2.1 Intro Screen
One screen before Word 1 appears. Brief, plain, no psychological framing. The intro screen prepares the user for the mechanic without explaining what the exercise is measuring.
Element
Spec
Header
'Word Association' — plain, medium weight. Same typographic treatment as other exercise titles.
Body copy
Exact text: 'You'll see one word at a time. Write the first thing that comes to mind — a word or short phrase. There are no right answers. Move quickly.' Four sentences. No more.
Start button
Full-width. Text: 'Begin'. Tapping loads Word 1.
Back option
None. The user has already unlocked this exercise. No exit from the intro screen back to dashboard — only forward.
DESIGNER NOTE

The intro copy says 'Move quickly' — this is the only behavioural instruction in the exercise. It is there because deliberation is the enemy of associative data. The design should reinforce this: the Begin button should be prominent, no decorative elements that invite lingering, no timer visible (which creates anxiety rather than speed). The instruction is verbal; the design is calm.
2.2 Word Screen — Layout and Behaviour
Each of the 12 words occupies its own screen. Layout is identical for all 12. The stimulus word is the dominant visual element. Everything else is minimal.
Element
Spec
Progress indicator
Top of screen. Format: '3 / 12'. Muted, small. Not a progress bar — just the fraction. No percentage, no animation.
Stimulus word

Large, centred, high contrast. Font size significantly larger than any other text on screen — this is the only thing the user should be looking at. All caps or title case (designer decision — hold consistently across all 12). Single word only, always on one line.
Input field

Below the stimulus word. Generous vertical space between word and field. Placeholder text: 'Type your response'. Single-line text field. Auto-focused on screen load — keyboard appears immediately without the user tapping the field.
Submit mechanic

Enter key on keyboard OR a visible Submit button below the field (both work). Tapping Enter or Submit locks the response and advances to the next word. Do not require both — Enter alone is sufficient on mobile keyboard.
Character limit
50 characters. Enough for a short phrase. Hard limit — field stops accepting input at 50. No error message — the field simply stops. This also prevents essays.
Minimum length
1 character. The user cannot submit an empty response. If the field is empty when Enter/Submit is triggered, do nothing — no error message, no shake animation. Just wait.
Back navigation
Not available. No back arrow. No swipe-back gesture (disable iOS/Android default swipe-back on this screen). Once a response is submitted, it is locked.
Word reveal animation

Optional: the stimulus word can fade in over 200ms on screen load. Not a requirement — but if any animation is used, it should be subtle and fast. No slide-in, no bounce, nothing that draws attention to itself.
DESIGNER NOTE

The keyboard should appear automatically when each word screen loads — the user should be able to start typing immediately without any tap. On iOS this requires the input field to receive programmatic focus on mount. On Android, use windowSoftInputMode adjustResize to prevent the keyboard from covering the stimulus word.
DEVELOPER NOTE

Disable swipe-back gesture for the duration of the exercise. In React Native: set gestureEnabled: false on the navigator for exercise screens. In Bubble native app: use a custom plugin or page lock. In web/PWA: intercept the popstate event. This is a data integrity requirement — a swipe-back mid-exercise produces an inconsistent response set.
2.3 Between Words — Transition

After the user submits a response, the next word appears. The transition should feel immediate — this is not a reflective pause, it is momentum. The goal is to keep the user in the associative flow state the intro screen primed.
Transition element
Spec
Timing
Next word appears within 100ms of submission. No deliberate pause or delay between words.
Previous response visibility

The previous stimulus word and response are NOT shown. The screen clears completely and the next word appears. The user should not be able to see what they wrote for Word 1 while responding to Word 2.
Animation
None, or a very fast fade (100ms) of the new word appearing. No transition animation between screens — the 'clearing' effect should feel like a cut, not a dissolve.
Progress indicator update
Updates immediately on the new screen — '4 / 12' appears at the same time as Word 4. Not animated separately.
2.4 Call 1 — Personalised Word Selection (Day 9)

Call 1 is a background API call that runs on Day 9 — one day before the exercise unlocks. The user never sees this call happen. It reads the user's first 9 journal entries and returns 2–3 personalised stimulus words that are inserted into the exercise sequence.
CALL 1 — PERSONALISED WORD SELECTION PROMPT

Here are a person's first 9 journal entries:
[entry_1_text] [entry_2_text] ...[entry_9_text]
Select 2–3 single words that meet ALL of the following criteria: 1. The word appeared in at least 2 of the 9 entries 2. The word carried visible emotional charge in the context it appeared — it was not neutral filler 3. The word is not in this list (fixed set): HOME, ANGER, ENOUGH, SAFE, WAITING, WRONG, CLOSE, STILL, BREAK 4. The word is not a proper noun (no names, places, brands) 5. The word is common enough that it functions as a clear stimulus — not so specific that it gives away what the system noticed 6. The word is NOT in this sensitivity exclusion list — these words are too raw to function as neutral projective stimuli: death, dead, dying, suicide, gone, leaving, alone, failure, worthless, abuse, trauma, hurt, lost, ending, nothing, hopeless, useless, empty, broken, ugly
Return only the words as a comma-separated list. No explanation. No preamble. No punctuation other than the comma separator.
If fewer than 2 words meet all criteria, return exactly 2 words that meet criteria 2–5 and 6, even if they only appeared once. If no words meet all criteria, return: CHANGE, LOSS
Scenario
What happens
Call 1 succeeds (2–3 words returned)

Words stored in draft ExerciseResult as personalised_words JSON array. Inserted into positions 3, 5, 9 of the 12-word sequence. Full sequence stored as word_sequence JSON array in draft ExerciseResult.
Call 1 returns fallback (CHANGE, LOSS)
CHANGE and LOSS are inserted at positions 3 and 5. Position 9 uses STILL (shifted). These are reasonable general stimuli — not as personalised but not harmful.
Call 1 fails / times out (8s)
Use CHANGE and LOSS as fallback — same as above. Do not block exercise unlock. Log the failure for review.
Fewer than 9 entries exist on Day 9 — prompt template adjustment required

Run Call 1 with however many entries exist — truncate the prompt template to include only [entry_1_text] through [entry_N_text] where N is the actual count. Do not include empty placeholder slots. If zero entries exist, use CHANGE and LOSS fallback immediately without calling the API. The selection criterion “appeared in at least 2 of the 9 entries” should be relaxed to “appeared in at least 2 entries” when fewer than 9 exist, and further relaxed to “appeared in at least 1 entry” when fewer than 4 entries exist.
Call 1 runs late (Day 9 trigger missed)

Run Call 1 when the user opens the exercise on Day 10 before showing the intro screen. Show a brief loading state: 'Preparing your exercise...' Do not show intro screen until Call 1 completes and word sequence is stored in draft ExerciseResult.
User closes app during inline Call 1 loading state

Draft ExerciseResult does NOT yet exist (Call 1 never completed). When user returns and opens the exercise again: no draft record exists, so inline Call 1 fires again from scratch. This is correct behaviour — treat it as a first open. The draft record is only created when Call 1 completes successfully. Do not attempt to resume a mid-Call-1 state.
DEVELOPER NOTE

Call 1 requires a scheduled backend trigger on Day 9. In Bubble, use a Scheduled API Workflow triggered when (Current Date/Time = User.program_start_date + 9 days). The trigger creates a draft ExerciseResult record for exercise_name = word_association with status = draft and stores the personalised words and full word sequence. The exercise unlock check on Day 10 reads from this draft record. If no draft record exists when the user opens the exercise, run Call 1 inline before showing the intro screen. BUBBLE SCHEDULING NOTE: Bubble Scheduled API Workflows cannot be triggered by a condition becoming true at an arbitrary future time. The correct pattern is: on Day 1 (when the user starts the program), schedule a Scheduled API Workflow to run at (program_start_date + 9 days). Do this in the same workflow that sets User.program_start_date. Do not attempt to use a recurring workflow that checks a condition — this is unreliable for per-user scheduling. If the Day 9 scheduled workflow is missed for any reason, the inline Call 1 fallback (run when user opens exercise on Day 10) handles recovery correctly.
2.5 Post-Exercise — Loading State and Call 2

After the user submits their response to Word 12 (the final word), the exercise transitions to a loading state while Call 2 runs. The loading state is brief and calm — it should not feel like waiting, it should feel like the exercise completing.
State
What happens
Immediate (0ms)
All 12 responses written to ExerciseResult.raw_responses JSON array. ExerciseResult.entry_count_at_completion written. Call 2 fires.
Loading state
Screen shows one line of text: 'Reading your responses.' No spinner. No percentage. Subtle fade-pulse on the text if animation is used.
Call 2 returns
AI analysis fields written to ExerciseResult (see Section 3). ExerciseResult.status set to completed. ExerciseResult.completed_at set. Screen transitions to Reflection Screen (Section 2.6).
Call 2 timeout (10s — longer than Call 1’s 8s because Call 2 processes all 12 stimulus-response pairs in a single analysis pass)

Write partial ExerciseResult with status = completed, ai_analysis_text = null. Route to Reflection Screen with fallback copy (Section 2.6). Do not block completion — the raw responses are the valuable data, the analysis is secondary.
2.6 Reflection Screen

The reflection screen shows the AI analysis output from Call 2. It is the final screen of the exercise. Unlike the OCEAN summary screen, the user may return to this screen — it is accessible from their exercise history. NOTE ON ISOLATION: Call 2 reads only the 12 stimulus-response pairs. It does not receive journal entries. The gap analysis between word association responses and journal language is deferred to the Day 30 report and weekly reports, where it has richer context to work with. The reflection screen shows what the responses reveal on their own terms.
Element
Spec
Header
Exercise name: 'Word Association'. Date completed below it, muted and small.
AI analysis text
The 2–3 sentence plain language output from Call 2. Medium-large text, generous white space. Not in a card — just text. Left-aligned.
Divider
Thin horizontal rule below the analysis text.
Feeds into note
One small muted line: 'This feeds into your Day 30 report.' No further explanation.
Done button
Full-width. Text: 'Done'. Returns user to the main dashboard / entry screen.
Fallback copy (if Call 2 timed out)
Replace AI analysis text with: 'Your responses have been recorded. They will feed into your Day 30 report.' No error message. No indication that something went wrong.
DESIGNER NOTE

The reflection screen is not a result or a score. It is a brief honest observation. The visual tone should match the daily reflection screens — same text treatment, same white space, same quiet register. The user should not feel like they received a verdict.
3. How It Is Stored

All Word Association data is stored in an ExerciseResult record. The draft record is created on Day 9 when Call 1 runs. It is completed on Day 10 when the user finishes the exercise and Call 2 returns.
3.1 ExerciseResult Fields — Word Association
Field
Type · Value · When written
exercise_name
Option Set value: word_association. Written on draft creation (Day 9).
exercise_number
Number: 1. Written on draft creation.
status
Option Set: draft → completed. Draft on Day 9. Completed after Call 2 returns on Day 10.
completed_at
Date/Time. Written when status changes to completed. This is the reference date for subsequent exercise unlock counting — critical.
word_sequence
Long Text. JSON array of 12 objects: [{position:1, word:'HOME', source:'fixed'}, {position:3, word:'work', source:'personalised'}, ...]. Written on Day 9 draft creation after Call 1.
personalised_words
Long Text. JSON array of 2–3 strings: ['work','tired'] — the words returned by Call 1. Stored separately for audit and quality review.
raw_responses

Long Text. JSON array of 12 objects: [{position:1, word:'HOME', response:'mum'}, {position:2, word:'ANGER', response:'buried'}, ...]. Written immediately after Word 12 is submitted, before Call 2 fires.
dominant_register
Option Set: threat / withdrawal / self-questioning / avoidant / direct / ambivalent. Written after Call 2.
emotional_register_gap
Option Set: match / partial / significant_gap. Written after Call 2. Feeds EI score calibration in Day 30 report.
suppression_flag
Yes/No. Written after Call 2. Set to Yes if significant_gap AND high-intensity emotional content in responses absent from entries. Feeds Branch C routing.
revealing_pairs
Long Text. JSON array of 2–3 objects: [{word:'WRONG', response:'always me', note:'self-blame present in responses but absent from entries'}]. Written after Call 2.
ai_analysis_text
Long Text. The 2–3 sentence plain language output from Call 2. Shown on Reflection Screen. Passed as context into Day 30 report prompt.
entry_count_at_completion
Number. Count of Entry records for this user at time of completion. Written immediately after Word 12 is submitted.
cycle_number
Number. Copied from User.cycle_number at completion.
3.2 Draft Record Lifecycle
Event
Record state
Day 9 — Call 1 fires
Draft ExerciseResult created. Fields written: exercise_name, exercise_number, status=draft, word_sequence, personalised_words.
Day 10 — User opens exercise
Draft record found. word_sequence read to build the exercise UI. No new record created.
Day 10 — Word 12 submitted
raw_responses and entry_count_at_completion written to existing draft record. Call 2 fires.
Day 10 — Call 2 returns
Remaining fields written: dominant_register, emotional_register_gap, suppression_flag, revealing_pairs, ai_analysis_text. Status set to completed. completed_at written.
Day 10 — Call 2 times out
status set to completed. completed_at written. AI fields left null. Entry unlock counting begins from completed_at regardless.
BUILD WARNING

completed_at must be written when the exercise is marked complete — not when the user taps Done on the Reflection Screen. The exercise is complete when Call 2 returns (or times out), not when the user acknowledges it. If completed_at is tied to the Done button tap, and the user doesn't tap Done, the next exercise will never unlock.
4. How It Is Used for Analysis and Interpretation
4.1 Call 2 — Analysis Prompt

Call 2 receives the 12 stimulus-response pairs only. Journal entries are not passed. It produces 2 short sentences addressed directly to the user, grounded in specific words and responses from the exercise, and populates the structured output fields. Gap analysis between word association and journal language is deferred to the Day 30 and weekly reports.
CALL 2 — ANALYSIS PROMPT

Personality context: [PERSONALITY_CONTEXT]
A person completed a word association exercise. Their 12 stimulus words and responses:
1. HOME → [response] 2. ANGER → [response] 3. [word_3] → [response] 4. ENOUGH → [response] 5. [word_5] → [response] 6. SAFE → [response] 7. WAITING → [response] 8. WRONG → [response] 9. [word_9] → [response] 10. CLOSE → [response] 11. STILL → [response] 12. BREAK → [response]
Do two things:
Write 2 short sentences to them using “you”.
Both sentences must reference specific words and responses from the list above. Do not make general observations. Do not summarise mood or feeling in the abstract. Every claim must be grounded in a specific word they were shown and what they said.
First sentence: name 2–3 specific responses and say what you notice about them together.
Second sentence: pick the single most interesting word-response pair. Name both. Say in one plain clause what it suggests.
Strict rules: - Must reference actual words from the list. No abstract observations. - No poetic or metaphorical language. Say it plainly. - No sentence like “you seem to be carrying something” or “there is something unresolved” — these are vague. Be specific. - “You” throughout. Never “this person”. - No jargon: register, avoidant, deflect, ambivalent, suppress, tension, dynamic, narrative, threshold, insight, unresolved, acute, ongoing, present. - No markdown, no bold, no asterisks. - Do not be warm or encouraging.
Good example: “SAFE got difficult, HOME got confusion, WAITING got forever — all three are things that should feel settled but you gave them all friction. The one that stands out is ENOUGH and you said peace, because that is the only word where you named something you want rather than something that is wrong.”
Bad example (do not write like this): “You seem to be carrying something that has not resolved yet — not acute, but present and ongoing.” This is bad because it says nothing specific. It could apply to anyone.
After your sentences, on a new line return only this JSON: {“dominant_register”: “[threat|withdrawal|self-questioning|avoidant|direct|ambivalent]”, “suppression_flag”: false, “revealing_pairs”: [{“word”: “[word]”, “response”: “[response]”, “note”: “[one sentence]”}]}
DEVELOPER NOTE

Call 2 returns both plain text and a JSON block. Parse these separately. The plain text (everything before the JSON block) goes into ai_analysis_text. The JSON block is parsed and its values written to the individual Option Set and Boolean fields.
If the JSON block is malformed or absent, do NOT leave structured fields null — use these explicit fallback values: dominant_register = ambivalent emotional_register_gap = partial suppression_flag = false revealing_pairs = []
Rationale: dominant_register and emotional_register_gap feed downstream routing and report generation. A null value will cause prompt assembly failures or silent misrouting. ambivalent and partial are the least committal valid values — they do not trigger branch flags or suppression logic, but they do not block anything either. Log the JSON parse failure for review.
A regex or split on the opening brace { handles the plain text / JSON separation reliably. If the response contains no { character at all, treat the entire response as plain text and apply fallback values to all structured fields. MARKDOWN STRIPPING: Despite the prompt instruction, the model may return bold or italic markdown in the plain text portion (e.g. **self-questioning**). Strip all markdown formatting from ai_analysis_text before storing and displaying: remove ** and * wrappers, remove # heading markers. Store and display plain prose only.
4.2 Register Interpretation — Internal Reference
These interpretations are used by the AI in Call 2 and by the Day 30 report prompt. They are not surfaced to the user.
Dominant register
Pattern in responses
Downstream implication
Threat / self-questioning
Responses cluster around danger, self-blame, negative self-assessment. HOME → 'complicated'. WRONG → 'always me'. BREAK → 'falling apart'.
High PR signal. Branch A or C candidate. Day 30 report probes whether the threat orientation is toward self or toward others.
Withdrawal / accommodation
Responses are soft, distancing, or people-pleasing. ANGER → 'not good'. CLOSE → 'careful'. SAFE → 'others first'.
High Agreeableness + withdrawal register = strong Branch C or Branch A candidate. Avoidance Audit and Unfinished Conversation exercises will be particularly resonant.
Direct expression
Responses are confident, specific, emotionally named. ANGER → 'when I feel dismissed'. HOME → 'where I recharge'. WRONG → 'I own it'.
Branch D candidate or healthy baseline. Day 30 report will check whether directness in word association matches directness in entries.
Avoidant detachment
Responses are abstract, structural, or deflecting. SAFE → 'a concept'. HOME → 'a place'. ANGER → 'emotion'.
Strongest suppression signal. Paired with significant_gap = automatic suppression_flag = true. Branch C primary candidate.
Ambivalent / mixed
No consistent pattern. Register shifts across words without a clear dominant tone.
Mixed signal — Day 30 report weights entry evidence more heavily. Branch routing deferred to SA and DT scores.
4.3 OCEAN Interaction with Call 2 Analysis
The OCEAN standing context block is prepended to the Call 2 prompt. It shapes two things in the analysis:
OCEAN signal
Effect on Call 2 analysis
High Neuroticism (>= 3.5)

Neutral or minimising responses (STILL → 'fine', BREAK → 'rest') are read with more suspicion — the neuroticism profile supports the inference that these may be understating reactivity. The gap assessment is more sensitive.
High Agreeableness (>= 3.5)

Withdrawal or accommodation responses are expected — the register is less surprising and therefore less diagnostic on its own. The gap assessment looks specifically at whether anger or frustration words appear in entries despite being deflected in responses.
Low Openness (< 2.5)
Abstract or detached responses are somewhat expected — low-openness users tend toward concrete thinking. Avoidant detachment register is weighted less heavily for suppression flagging.
High Openness (>= 3.5)
Ambivalent or conceptual responses may reflect genuine complexity rather than avoidance. Mixed register is interpreted more charitably.
5. How It Feeds Into Weekly and Monthly Reports
5.1 Weekly Report — Week 1 (The Week Exercise 1 Completes)
Exercise 1 completes on Day 10, which falls in Week 2 of the program. The weekly report for Week 2 includes an Exercise This Week section referencing it.
Weekly report section
What Exercise 1 feeds into it
Exercise This Week

Shows: exercise name ('Word Association · Completed Day 10'), the most revealing pair identified by the AI ('When shown WRONG, you wrote always me'), and a one-sentence observation connecting it to the week's entry language. Shows: 'Feeds into Day 30 report' label.
Emotion Language This Week

The dominant_register from Exercise 1 is passed into the weekly report AI prompt as context. It calibrates which related words are surfaced in the word family section — see EX-00 Section 4.4 for the OCEAN × Emotion Language interaction. The Exercise 1 register adds a second layer: a threat/self-questioning register user seeing 'tired' in their entries will have 'exhausted, depleted' surfaced with more confidence.
What We Saw

The revealing_pairs from Exercise 1 are passed into the weekly report AI prompt. The AI may reference them if they connect to patterns visible in Week 2 entries — e.g. 'Your entries this week circled the same territory your Word Association responses pointed at.'
Carry Into Next Week

If a significant_gap was flagged, the weekly report carry-forward question is more likely to name the gap directly: 'Your entries say tired. Your associations went somewhere else. What's the word you're not using?'
5.2 Weekly Reports — Weeks 3 Onwards

Exercise 1 data does not generate a new Exercise This Week section after Week 2 — it is complete. But its outputs remain as standing context in all subsequent weekly report prompts for the duration of Cycle 1:
dominant_register passed as standing context — shapes Emotion Language word family prioritisation every week
emotional_register_gap passed as standing context — informs whether the AI treats entry language at face value or probes beneath it
revealing_pairs passed as standing context — available for the AI to reference when entry patterns connect
suppression_flag passed as standing context — activates more careful treatment of emotional flatness in entries throughout Cycle 1
5.3 Monthly Report Feed
Exercise 1 outputs are passed into every monthly report prompt throughout Cycle 1 and beyond as part of the baseline context block.
Monthly report section
What Exercise 1 feeds
Dimension score narratives

emotional_register_gap is a direct input to EI score calibration. A significant_gap user's EI score narrative acknowledges that entries may be underrepresenting what is present. A match user's EI score is taken more at face value.
Pattern tracking

dominant_register is referenced when monthly reports track whether the user's emotional language in entries is becoming more aligned with their associative register over time. 'Your entries in Month 3 are beginning to use language closer to what your Word Association responses pointed at' is a meaningful tracking statement.
Branch pattern narrative

suppression_flag feeds Branch C narrative framing throughout the year. Monthly reports for Branch C users reference the flag when describing why the platform is attentive to physical signals and indirect language.
5.4 Day 30 Report Feed
Exercise 1 is one of three exercises that feed the Day 30 report (along with Exercise 2 and Exercise 3). Its specific contributions:
Day 30 report section
Exercise 1 contribution
EI Score calibration

emotional_register_gap is the primary calibrator. A significant_gap shifts EI score upward — the user's actual emotional intensity is likely higher than entries alone suggest. A match confirms the EI score derived from entry language.
Self-Perception Gap section

The revealing_pairs are shown verbatim in the Exercise section of the Day 30 report — stimulus word and the user's exact response, no paraphrasing. Format: 'WRONG → always me'. The AI then contrasts this against entry language in a separate sentence below each pair. The user sees what they actually wrote, not a summary of it. This is a product decision: showing the verbatim response is more confronting and more honest than paraphrasing it.
Branch routing narrative

dominant_register + suppression_flag inform how the branch assignment is explained. Not as routing inputs — routing is driven by EI/PR/SA/DT scores — but as dispositional context that makes the assignment make sense in plain language.
Standing context for subsequent exercises

ai_analysis_text and revealing_pairs are passed into every subsequent exercise AI prompt as part of the Cycle 1 baseline context block. The Avoidance Audit, Cost-Benefit Audit, and Unfinished Conversation exercise prompts all have access to what Exercise 1 found.
6. Additional Considerations
6.1 Word Sequence Design — Why This Order
The 9 fixed words are not in a random order. The sequence is designed to create a rhythm that makes the most revealing responses available before the user has time to build a strategy.
Position rationale
Design logic
Position 1: HOME
Warm, relatively safe entry point. Almost everyone has an immediate association. Sets the typing rhythm without threatening anything.
Position 2: ANGER

Second word is more confronting than first. Coming immediately after HOME creates a juxtaposition — safety followed by the word most people have a complicated relationship with. The contrast is deliberate.
Position 3: Personalised

After two fixed words the user has a rhythm. The personalised word feels continuous — it appears to be another 'normal' word in the sequence. Its familiarity (it came from their own writing) makes it more likely to produce an instinctive response.
Positions 4–6: ENOUGH, Personalised, SAFE
Middle section. Three words covering adequacy, something personally charged, and safety. The sequence doesn't feel like a pattern — which is the point.
Positions 7–8: WAITING, WRONG

The two most directly self-referential fixed words. By position 7 the user is in a rhythm and less likely to deliberate. WRONG at position 8 — rather than earlier — means the self-blame probe arrives when deliberation is lowest.
Position 9: Personalised
Third personalised word in the final third. By now the user is moving quickly. The familiar word produces a less guarded response than it would at position 3.
Positions 10–12: CLOSE, STILL, BREAK

Closing trio. CLOSE probes relational proximity, STILL asks how rest is experienced, BREAK lands last — the word most likely to reveal rupture vs. rest orientation. Ending on BREAK means any rupture associations surface at the point of lowest guard.
6.2 Response Quality — What to Do With Non-Responses

Some users will submit responses that are not genuine associations — a single letter, a period, the word 'skip', or a repetition of the stimulus word. These are data too, but they need to be handled without disrupting the exercise.
Response type
How it is handled
Single character (e.g. '.' or 'x')
Accepted as valid. Stored as-is. The Call 2 prompt notes these as minimal responses. A user who submits single characters consistently is showing avoidance of the exercise itself — that is a signal.
Repetition of stimulus word (e.g. HOME → 'home')
Accepted as valid. Stored as-is. Call 2 is instructed to treat repetitions as deflections — the user did not produce an association, they reflected the stimulus back. This is flagged in the analysis.
Clearly unrelated (e.g. numbers, gibberish)
Accepted as valid. The minimum viable response is 1 character. The exercise does not validate response quality. Call 2 handles unusual responses in its analysis.
All 12 responses are minimal or deflecting
Call 2 will note this pattern. emotional_register_gap is likely to be set to significant_gap. The AI analysis will reference the pattern without shaming it.
DEVELOPER NOTE

Do not build response validation logic that tries to detect 'bad' responses. Any 1+ character response is valid. The quality assessment belongs to the AI, not to the form validation layer. The only validation the form does: field cannot be empty on submit.
6.3 What Happens If the User Abandons Mid-Exercise
Drop point
What happens
User drops before Word 1 (on intro screen)

Draft ExerciseResult exists (created Day 9). Status remains draft. raw_responses is empty. When user returns, exercise restarts from intro screen. Word sequence is already stored in draft record — no need to re-run Call 1.
User drops mid-exercise (Words 1–11)

Draft ExerciseResult exists. raw_responses contains partial responses. When user returns, exercise restarts from Word 1 — not from where they left off. Partial responses are overwritten when new responses are submitted.
User drops after Word 12 but before Call 2 completes

raw_responses is written (fires on Word 12 submission). Call 2 may or may not have completed. When user returns: if ai_analysis_text is written, show Reflection Screen. If not, re-fire Call 2 with stored raw_responses and entry data, then show Reflection Screen.
BUILD WARNING

Do NOT resume mid-exercise from the last answered word. The associative quality of the exercise depends on completing it in a single sitting. A user who drops at Word 7 and resumes the next day is not in the same mental state — the responses would not be comparable to Words 1–6. Always restart from Word 1 if the exercise was abandoned mid-flow.
6.4 Personalised Words — Privacy and Sensitivity
Call 1 reads the user's first 9 journal entries to select personalised words. Two sensitivity considerations:
Consideration
Handling
The selected word reveals what the system noticed

By design, the user doesn't know which words are personalised. But if a user has been writing about 'work' and 'work' appears in the exercise, they may recognise it. This is acceptable — the recognition itself often produces a more genuine response. It is not a privacy issue, it is a feature working as intended.
Call 1 processes entry text via API

Entry content is sent to the AI API for word selection. This is the same privacy consideration as the daily reflection API calls — journal entry content is processed by the AI. This should be disclosed in the product's privacy policy and terms of service, not handled at the exercise level.
6.5 Second Cycle Behaviour

Exercise 1 runs only in Cycle 1. It is not repeated in Cycle 2 or beyond. The dominant_register and emotional_register_gap established in Cycle 1 carry forward as standing context into Cycle 2 prompts as baseline data. If the product eventually introduces a Cycle 2 version of Exercise 1, it would compare new responses against the Cycle 1 baseline — but this is not built in v1.
